title: Beyond parameters: I/O, files, exceptions and fixtures
summary: Real methods read keyboards and files, print to screens, and throw exceptions. Learn to simulate inputs, capture outputs, test files and exceptions, and share setup with fixtures.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: So far every method looked like a maths function: parameters in, return value out. Real methods are messier. Their data can come from the keyboard, fields, files, databases or the network, and their results can go to the screen, files, or other programs as well as return values. These side effects still need testing, which means test code must control the inputs and observe the outputs without changing the production code. Console input, console output, file reads and file writes all share one convenient fact: everything is a string, with newline characters separating lines.

sections.heading: Simulating console input
paras: To test a method that reads the keyboard, hand it a fake keyboard: create an object holding your scripted input string and tell the system to read from it instead of the console. Python sets sys.stdin to an io.StringIO holding e.g. 10\n20; Java calls System.setIn with a ByteArrayInputStream of the same bytes. The production method cannot tell the difference, so the inputMax test feeds 10\n20 and expects 20 back, exactly as if a user had typed it.

sections.heading: Capturing console output
paras: Output is the mirror image: redirect the screen into a buffer, run the method, then read the buffer back. Python points sys.stdout at an io.StringIO and later calls getvalue(); Java points System.setOut at a PrintStream over a ByteArrayOutputStream and reads toString(). The outputMax test therefore calls outputMax(10, 15) and asserts the captured text is 15. Input and output redirection compose: a method that both prompts and prints gets both treatments at once.

sections.heading: Testing file handling
paras: Files work the same way, except setup and verification move outside the call. To test a reader, the test first writes the input file (e.g. inputfile.txt containing 10\n15), then calls the method and checks the return. To test a writer, the test calls the method first, then opens the produced file and asserts on its contents (stripping trailing newlines before comparing). Python uses open and with blocks; Java uses PrintWriter/Scanner with explicit close. The rule never changes: prepare the world, run, then verify.

sections.heading: Expected versus unexpected exceptions
paras: Exceptions need care because they invert pass and fail. An unexpected exception, whether from broken test code or faulty production, should fail the test; in Python you simply let it propagate, in Java you declare throws on the test method. An expected exception is the opposite: the method should throw (for instance formatTime raising on invalid input instead of returning an error string), so the test only passes if the exception arrives. The pattern is a try block ending in assert False (reached only when nothing threw) with the pass sitting in the except/catch clause.

sections.heading: Fixtures: setUp and tearDown
paras: Redirected streams and scratch files must not leak between tests, so every suite shares the same setup and cleanup. A test fixture is everything put in place to make a test work in isolation, and the convention is two helpers: setUp() runs immediately before every test method, tearDown() immediately after. Without a framework you call them around each test by hand; with Python unittest you define setUp/tearDown methods and with JUnit you annotate them @Before/@After, and the framework calls them automatically. TearDown restores the original System.in/System.out and deletes scratch files, so the next test starts clean.

callout.text: Worksheet 10 is the template for any I/O exam question: identify paths, choose inputs (params, console string or file contents) per path, state expected returns, exceptions, console text or file text, then implement with redirection plus setUp/tearDown.

recall.q: How do you test a method that reads from the keyboard?
recall.a: Simulate the input: put the scripted string (with \n between lines) in an io.StringIO / ByteArrayInputStream and install it as sys.stdin / System.in before calling. The method reads it exactly as typed input.

recall.q: How do you test a method that prints to the screen?
recall.a: Capture the output: redirect sys.stdout / System.out to a buffer, call the method, then assert on the buffer contents (getvalue() / toString()). Restore the real streams in tearDown.

recall.q: What is a test fixture, and what do setUp/tearDown do?
recall.a: A fixture is everything arranged to run a test in isolation. setUp() runs before every test (redirect streams, create files) and tearDown() runs after (restore streams, delete files). Frameworks (unittest setUp/tearDown, JUnit @Before/@After) call them automatically.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 6-16 (Beyond params/returns; newlines; simulating input)
citations.excerpt: Methods take data from keyboards, fields, files and more, and send results to screens and files as side effects. Console traffic is one big string with newline separators. Tests simulate input with sys.stdin/io.StringIO in Python and System.setIn/ByteArrayInputStream in Java.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 23-37 (Capturing output; file read/write tests)
citations.excerpt: Capture screen output by redirecting sys.stdout/System.setOut to a buffer and reading it back. To test file readers, write the input file first; to test writers, read the output file afterwards and assert on its contents.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 38-49 (Expected vs unexpected exceptions; fixtures, setUp/tearDown)
citations.excerpt: Unexpected exceptions should fail the test; expected exceptions must arrive or the test fails (try with assert False, pass in except/catch). setUp() runs before every test and tearDown() after; unittest uses setUp/tearDown names while JUnit uses @Before/@After.

visuals.title: The fixture lifecycle
visuals.what: Isolation by construction: every test builds its world and cleans it up.

steps.title: setUp
steps.text: Redirect streams, create input files before every test.

steps.title: Call
steps.text: Run production with the planned data.

steps.title: Verify
steps.text: Assert returns, exceptions, console text or file text.

steps.title: tearDown
steps.text: Restore streams, delete scratch files after every test.
